where: Section 3, Choosing a model (repeated in Quiz Q6 answer)
problem: The text says a publish-subscribe broker 'sends only when a value changes'. That is not how a broker works. The broker forwards every message it receives to all current subscribers. Deciding to publish only on a change is the publisher's choice (event-driven reporting), not a broker feature. A sensor that publishes the same 31.5 °C every 10 s still causes the broker to forward every one of those messages.
fix: Write: 'A publish-subscribe broker forwards every message it is given, so the publisher decides how often to publish — often only when a value changes. If the broker keeps the last message (the retained message in MQTT), a new subscriber gets that value at once. The cost is a broker to run and secure.' Make the same correction in the Q6 answer: 'the sensor publishes once per update instead of answering 500 queries'.

problem: The example body {value: 31.5, unit: °C} is not valid JSON. Object keys must be quoted strings, and °C must be a string value.
The actors are listed as ['Device', 'API server', 'Client'], so the Client sits on the far right and every arrow runs right-to-left, against the reading order of the caption.
fix: Order the actors ['Client', 'API server', 'Device'] so the call reads left to right.

problem: 'Forgetting the response halves the load' is not generally true; the error depends on the size ratio. In worked example 1, counting only the 300-byte requests gives 5.4 MB per hour instead of 14.4 MB, which is far more than a factor of two.
fix: Say: 'Forgetting the response under-counts badly. In worked example 1 it gives 5.4 MB instead of 14.4 MB per hour.'

problem: The sentence 'The API style and the communication model must agree' is contradicted by the example that follows it, where a REST endpoint behind a publish-subscribe broker is still request-response. A student will not know which rule to keep.
fix: Rewrite: 'The API style fixes what the client sees, not what sits behind it. A REST endpoint backed by a broker is still request-response for the client, unless the client itself subscribes to a topic.'

problem: The answer says publish-subscribe 'removes 500 separate polling requests per second', which is true, but it does not mention that the broker still delivers one copy of each update to each of the 500 viewers. The fan-out traffic to the viewers does not disappear.
fix: Add: 'The saving is on the upstream side — one publish instead of 500 requests. The broker still sends one copy to each of the 500 subscribers per update, so downstream traffic per viewer stays roughly the same.'
